explanation:
## The program

```cpp
while (std::cin >> x)
{
    if (count == 0) { lowest = x; highest = x; }
    else
    {
        if (x < lowest)  lowest = x;
        if (x > highest) highest = x;
    }
    ++count;
}
```

## while (std::cin >> x)

`std::cin >> x` is an expression whose value is the stream, and a
stream converts to `bool` as "am I still usable". So the condition
means: read the next number, and keep going if that worked.

It fails on end of input and on malformed input alike, which is
usually what you want for a filter reading numbers and sometimes
not — a program that must tell "no more data" from "that was not a
number" has to look at `std::cin.eof()` and `std::cin.fail()`
separately afterwards.

What you must not write is:

```cpp
while (!std::cin.eof())     // wrong
{
    std::cin >> x;
    // ...
}
```

`eof()` reports that a *previous* read hit the end, so this runs the
body one extra time with `x` holding whatever the failed read left
behind. Test the read, not the flag.

## The starting value problem

A sum starts at 0 and a product starts at 1, because those are the
values that leave the answer unchanged — the identity for the
operation. Minimum has no such value among the `int`s: whatever you
pick, some input is smaller.

There are three ways out, and they are worth knowing apart:

1. **Use the first element.** What the reference does. It is correct
   for every input and needs the "have I seen one yet" test, which
   the count supplies for free.
2. **Start at the extreme of the type**, `std::numeric_limits<int>
   ::max()` from `<limits>`. Correct for `int`, and it quietly
   answers "what is the minimum of nothing" with a very large
   number, which is a lie that looks like data.
3. **Start at 0.** Wrong, and the test that catches it is a set of
   all-negative numbers — which is why there is one above.

## One pass, three answers

All three are accumulated in the same loop. That matters more than
it looks: the input here is a stream, and a stream can only be read
once. Three separate loops would need the numbers stored first —
which is fine for a thousand of them and not for a billion.

## What this does not check

The difference between "the input ended" and "the input contained a
word". Both stop the loop, and both are reported as however many
numbers were read before that point. A program validating its input
would have to separate them.
